rationale: The book's definition of the Sabbath as the complete unit of seven (the week itself) provides a unified, literal explanation for textual features that the traditional view must explain away as metonymy or redundancy. Specifically, it directly accounts for the phrase 'day of the sabbath' (parallel to 'day of the new moon'), the literal Greek phrasing 'twice in the sabbath' (Luke 18:12) and 'one of the sabbaths' (Matthew 28:1), and the application of the term to the forty-nine-year Jubilee cycle as 'seven sabbaths of years' (Leviticus 25:8).
book_core_identification: The Sabbath is a complete unit of seven at any scale (days, weeks, years) of which the resting element is the completing member, rather than exclusively naming the single day of rest itself.
book_secondary_elaborations: It operates at every scale the law counts, including the land's seventh year and the seven sevens to Jubilee.
Hebrew counts 'seven sabbaths' (shabbatot) where Deuteronomy counts the same span as 'seven weeks' (shavuot).
Greek uses the word sabbath to name the week, as in 'twice in the sabbath' (twice a week) and 'one of the sabbaths' (first day of the week).
The rest is the completing member of the whole unit.
chapter_only_objections: The chapter argues that the biblical calendar is non-continuous, utilizing intercalated new moon days that break the seven-day cycle to ensure the 15th is always a weekly Sabbath. This is highly contentious and relies on complex deductions about the Omer count.
The claim that a continuous seven-day week makes the qualifier 'complete' (temimot) mathematically meaningless in the Omer count.
strongest_counter_interpretation: The word 'Sabbath' primarily means the seventh day of rest or cessation. Because this day anchors and defines the seven-day cycle, the name of the day came to be used by synecdoche/metonymy for the entire week in both Hebrew and Greek idioms.
counter_core_identification: The Sabbath is primarily the seventh day of rest, with its application to the week being a derived metonymy.
material_core_denial: The book denies that Sabbath primarily names the day, instead asserting its primary structural referent is the complete unit of seven.
counter_case: A day of rest is the most prominent feature of the biblical week, making metonymy (naming the whole by its defining part) an entirely natural and common linguistic development.
The root of the word (shavat) means to cease or rest, which directly describes the day of cessation, not intrinsically the six days of labor that precede it.
The command 'Remember the sabbath day' (Exodus 20:8) focuses on the day itself as the specific object of memorial and hallowing.
book_explanatory_advantages: Explains the grammar of 'day of the sabbath' (yom ha-shabbat) as a possessive construct mapping a day to a unit, parallel to 'day of the new moon' (yom ha-chodesh), rather than treating it as a redundancy.
Explains the literal use of the word for week-long spans without invoking figures of speech (e.g., 'twice in the sabbath', 'seven sabbaths of years').
Explains why the law counts 'seven sabbaths' and demands they be 'complete'—a span can be whole or broken; a single day cannot be partially itself.
Explains the doubling of the word ('shabbat shabbaton') for the rest day itself, distinguishing the specific resting member from the broader unit.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Aligns directly with the etymology of the verb 'shavat' (to cease/rest).
Avoids the need to restructure the historical calendar to accommodate 'broken' weeks, which the book's full chapter application heavily relies upon.
decisive_sources: Leviticus 25:8 (demonstrates the term scales mathematically as a unit of seven years)
unresolved_objections: The etymology of 'shabbat' links strongly to cessation, which characterizes the seventh day but not the six days of labor included in the unit.

The chapter's broader lunar-sabbath calendar theory (though excluded from the glossary scope ruling) would face severe historical and traditional objections that remain unaddressed in the provided text.
